If we bring him back through the gate like this...” She didn’t finish the thought. Meg rubbed her face and let out a sharp breath. “So, what are you saying? We just leave him here? ” “ Obviously not.” Claudette snapped at her, “But I’m not seeing a way to get him back to the campfire without risking a complete collapse that we can’t fix. Even if a hatch opened right here so we didn’t have to move him, the Fog would bring him back in who knows what condition. It barely manages to clear normal injuries when we leave. And if we get him back and he dies at camp, then what? There’s no precedent for that! We have no idea what would happen!” She rocked back on her heels, hands clenched in her lap, fighting the sinking dread curling at her edges. “I don’t know what to do here.” Jake had been quiet while the girls spoke, chewing over every word like they might unstick something in his brain. Each option seemed just as bad as the last. The hatch and the gate were both off the table—too risky, too uncertain. Either path meant dragging Leon out of the trial and hoping the Fog did something merciful, but the odds were grim. Claudette was right. The Fog was finicky even on a good day. Unreliable. It barely cleaned up normal wounds. And this? This was a total system failure. Although... His fingers curled tight against his knee, jaw tight as he worked through the other half of the thought — the one he didn’t want to say out loud yet. There was a point where it worked overtime on someone, fixing trial injuries so efficiently that it sometimes would repair damage that even the survivor didn’t know they had. It was relatively consistent. Reliable. A complete rebuild from scratch. Not kind, clearly, but practical — the Entity can’t run a trial if there are no pieces on the board, afterall. His stomach twisted. The logic was sound. But the cost? He dragged a hand down his face. Meg was going to punch him. And Claudette might just join her. He ran the loop again, trying to find another route. A loophole. Anything to avoid the conclusion he kept circling back to. But no matter how many times he ran it, the result was always the same. This was the only option that might work. And it sucked. God, it sucked so bad. Jake exhaled slowly, pushing himself to his feet. His hands were slick, but he wiped them against his jeans like that would steady him. It didn’t. “We do have one more option, here.” Jake looked between them, then down at Leon, avoiding the gaze of the girls. If he didn’t look right at them, maybe he wouldn’t lose his nerve. “If the Entity takes someone as a sacrifice... the Fog has to rebuild them. Completely. It doesn’t have a choice. Otherwise, there’s nothing left to throw into the next trial.” Meg stared at him, appalled. “A hook death ? You’re seriously talking about sacrificing him?” Jake ran a hand through his hair, trying to think. “I mean, do you have a better idea? Hook deaths bring a person back to the campfire a lot more whole than escaping out the gate does half the time. It likely won’t fix everything, but it’s a lot more efficient than anything else we have available right now.” A heavy silence fell between them. Meg stared out the doorway like the wall might offer her a rebuttal, but her jaw stayed locked. Jake crouched beside Leon, studying his face. His skin was pale and blotchy in strange patches. The bruising from the cuff had spread in streaks along the electricity burns. He hadn’t come around, but Jake knew Leon would be on his side here. He was practical, quick to take action once a viable path had shown itself. Claudette chewed her lip nervously, mentally mapping out the area. It was a terrible idea, but then again, so was every other one they had come up with. Plus, Jake’s idea at least had a track record. They had all seen it. The hook deaths were horrible to experience, but you always came back with much less physical injury than if you had just escaped or bled out. It could work. But they would have to haul Leon between the three of them, and the closest hook she could remember was several rooms over with a very angry psychopath on the prowl. "None of us can carry him. Not that far." “Oh, don’t tell me even YOU’RE considering this, now?” Meg turned on her, clearly at the limit of her tolerance. The trial had already gone to hell. Now they were just... sitting in a crumbling waiting room, debating the logistics of killing one of their own like it was a strategy meeting? And worse — Claudette’s lack of outrage was only bolstering Jake. His anxious fidgeting was evolving into measured pacing, thoughts coalescing into something more than just theory. “He’d never make it to a hook, not without help. He can’t walk. Can barely breathe. None of us can move him fast or quiet enough.” “And even if we could, we have no way of getting him up there,” Claudette flashed an apologetic look at Meg. “Besides, as far as we know, survivors can’t sacrifice each other. Probably why the Entity keeps the hooks so high up.” “It has to be a killer. The Doctor would have to do it.” Meg choked back a manic laugh — dry and bitter — at the absolute insanity of it all.
